damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 — Malfoy confronts Harry near the tree before the ferret transformation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 149: Malfoy provokes Harry with quiet menace and genuine courage: 'Go on, then, Potter. Moody's not here to look after you now - do it, if you've got the guts.' He draws his own wand and meets Harry in a mutual duel. He is calculating and bold, not merely a taunting bystander.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3: Malfoy calls down from a tree ('Why so tense, Potter?'), delivers a boast about a bet with his father ('He thinks you won't last five'), and is caught off-guard by Moody's transformation. He is passive and smug, with no wand drawn, no direct confrontation, and no mutual escalation — he is simply punished for mocking Harry.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book establishes Malfoy as genuinely dangerous and bold enough to draw his wand and challenge Harry directly. The film reduces this to schoolyard taunting from a safe perch up a tree, stripping away his menace and replacing it with buffoonery. His characterisation shifts from calculated rival to comic punchline even before the ferret scene begins.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 — The ferret transformation sequence
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 106–121: Malfoy had just attacked Harry from behind (a cowardly act Moody explicitly condemns), is bounced painfully as a ferret, shows watering eyes of 'pain and humiliation', mutters about his father under his breath, and is marched off by Moody. His humiliation is real but contextualised: it follows a genuine act of cowardice on his part.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scenes 3–4: The ferret scene is played almost entirely for slapstick comedy — 'Moody' winks at Harry who laughs, the ferret is sent up a friend's trouser leg for extended physical comedy. Malfoy simply runs away afterward. The moral context (punishing a cowardly sneak attack) is absent because the film did not show Malfoy attacking Harry from behind. The scene becomes pure humiliation spectacle rather than a consequence of Malfoy's cowardice.
damaging_scenes.explanation: By omitting the backstory of Malfoy's cowardly attack on Harry, the film turns a morally loaded punishment into pure comedy at Malfoy's expense. This flattens him from a character who earns his comeuppance into a simple butt of a joke, reducing audience understanding of his nature as a bully who strikes from behind.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Malfoy and Lucius at the Quidditch World Cup Top Box
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 4–16: Draco 'settled himself between his mother and father' and 'shot Harry, Ron, and Hermione one contemptuous look' after watching the Weasley confrontation. The book depicts him as a silent, contemptuous presence absorbing his father's social dominance and class cruelty — his contempt is directed at all three, including Hermione ('Mudblood' dynamic is contextualised).
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1: Lucius delivers the 'put it this way: if it rains, you'll be the first to know' line and 'Don't boast, Draco. There's no need with these people.' Draco's only line is boasting about the Minister's box. He is immediately silenced and diminished by his father in front of Harry. The dynamic is almost entirely Lucius-driven; Draco is a prop used to establish Lucius's condescension.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's World Cup encounter shows Draco as a semi-independent actor — contemptuous, watching, making his own judgements. The film collapses him into a subordinate whose boasting is publicly corrected by his father. While Lucius's 'don't boast' line exists to belittle the Weasleys, its side effect is establishing Draco as meek and easily silenced by his father even in a brief encounter, which undermines his independent menace.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 — Absence of Malfoy's encounter with Harry, Ron, and Hermione in the woods during the Death Eater riot
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 19–38: One of the most defining Malfoy scenes in Goblet of Fire. Draco stands alone, 'leaning against a tree, looking utterly relaxed', and delivers a sustained, layered performance: he warns Hermione (ambiguously, possibly genuinely) that the Death Eaters are targeting Muggles while simultaneously using 'Mudblood', taunts Harry about his father's possible involvement ('Well... if they were, I wouldn't be likely to tell you, would I, Potter?'), and shows cold, composed awareness of events that implicates his family. This scene establishes his ambiguity, his class cruelty, his intelligence, and his uneasy position regarding the Death Eaters.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 2: This scene is entirely absent. The woods riot shows only Death Eaters marching, Barty Crouch Jr. casting the Dark Mark, and Arthur finding the trio. Malfoy does not appear.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the single most damaging omission in the corpus. The woods encounter is the only scene in the book where Malfoy's relationship to Voldemort's cause is explored with ambiguity — he is complicit, informed, and cruel, but also implicitly aware of danger and capable of a twisted kind of warning. Its removal erases all suggestion that Draco knows more than he admits about his family's allegiances, which is foundational to his arc across the saga. The film's Draco has no connection whatsoever to the Death Eater subplot that dominates the novel.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 — Absence of Malfoy's 'POTTER STINKS' badge campaign and the corridor confrontation with Hermione's teeth
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 144–164: Malfoy actively produces and distributes anti-Harry badges, calls Hermione a 'Mudblood' to her face while offering her a badge, draws his wand and challenges Harry to a duel, fires 'Densaugeo' at Hermione (causing her teeth to grow), and then smugly flashes 'POTTER STINKS' in Snape's class. This sequence establishes Malfoy's sustained campaign of targeted cruelty, his willingness to use Dark-adjacent magic against Hermione specifically, and his cowardice in exploiting Snape's protection.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3: The badges appear briefly (students wearing them insult Harry in the corridor, a close-up shows the badge flipping to 'Potter Stinks'), but the entire wand-duel, Hermione's injury, Snape's classroom aftermath, and Malfoy's targeted use of 'Mudblood' slurs are absent. The badges function as background set-dressing rather than evidence of Malfoy's active, vicious campaign.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's badge sequence is the primary vehicle for showing Malfoy's sustained, inventive cruelty toward Harry and his targeted malice toward Hermione as a Muggle-born. By reducing it to background atmosphere, the film removes Malfoy's agency as an active antagonist during the tournament period and eliminates the specific injury to Hermione that book-readers remember as one of his most vindictive acts.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 — Absence of Malfoy's exploitation of the Rita Skeeter / Daily Prophet articles against Harry and Hagrid
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 176, 191–206: Malfoy 'was still quoting Rita Skeeter's article to him at every possible opportunity'; he gleefully produces the Skeeter article exposing Hagrid's giant heritage ('Hate to break it to you, Potter'), taunts Harry about his mental health ('Hey, Potter! How's your head?'), and whispers 'Missing your half-breed pal?' to Harry when teachers are nearby so he can't retaliate. These scenes show Malfoy as a strategic, persistent tormentor who uses information and social/media power rather than only direct confrontation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film corpus: None of this material appears. Rita Skeeter exists in the film (Scene 4) but her articles are discussed by Hermione and Ron without Malfoy weaponising them. Malfoy's campaign against Hagrid is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: These scenes establish Malfoy's intelligence and his strategic exploitation of institutional and media power — traits that become critical to understanding him in later books. Their absence leaves the film's Malfoy as a purely physical/verbal bully with no capacity for the kind of cold, calculated cruelty the books establish.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 — Malfoy slaps a Slytherin boy after the second task
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 254–257: At the end-of-year ceremony, Malfoy mutters to Crabbe and Goyle during Dumbledore's speech about Cedric's death, and remains defiantly seated with goblet untouched when Dumbledore toasts Harry. His response to the return of Voldemort is contemptuous silence and defiance — measured, political, chilling.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 5: After the second task scores are announced, Malfoy slaps a boy who was cheering for Harry. This is an impulsive, petty act of physical violence against a subordinate — no equivalent exists in the book corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The slap is a small invented moment, but it substitutes crude physical aggression for the book's more chilling portrait of Malfoy as someone whose menace is political and ideological rather than impulsively violent. It makes him seem like a petulant thug rather than the cold, class-conscious operator the books establish. Low damage overall but a misrepresentation of his character register.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3/4 — Absence of the train compartment confrontation at the end of year
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 263–281: In the final Hogwarts Express scene, Malfoy enters with a 'smirk quivering on his lips', delivers his most ideologically explicit speech of the book ('You've picked the losing side, Potter... They'll be the first to go, now the Dark Lord's back!'), is hexed by Harry, Ron, Hermione, Fred, and George simultaneously, and is left unconscious with tentacles on his face, then kicked into the corridor. This scene closes his arc for the year: he has shown his hand regarding Voldemort's return and been defeated collectively.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film corpus: This scene does not appear. The film ends without any closing confrontation with Malfoy on the train.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The train confrontation is the only scene in the book where Malfoy explicitly aligns himself with Voldemort's return and is made to pay a direct consequence for it. Its absence means the film's Malfoy has no arc-closing moment that foreshadows his role in Order of the Phoenix and Half-Blood Prince. The audience loses the signal that he is not merely a school bully but a character whose family allegiance will define his future trajectory.

main_damage_causes: Omission of the Death Eater riot woods encounter, which is the only scene establishing Malfoy's ambiguous complicity in his family's allegiances and his capacity for morally complex behaviour
Reduction of Malfoy's sustained antagonist campaign (badges, Hermione's injury, Hagrid articles) to background atmosphere, stripping his agency and strategic intelligence as a villain
Loss of the train compartment finale, which closes his year-long arc by explicitly connecting him to Voldemort's return and foreshadowing his future role in the saga
